title: Longest Common Subsequence
description:
Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their longest **common subsequence**. A subsequence keeps the relative order of characters but may skip any of them. If the strings share no characters, return `0`.

For example, `"ace"` is a subsequence of `"abcde"`, but `"aec"` is not.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Compare the last characters of both strings. If they match, they can both be part of the answer.

Let dp[i][j] be the LCS length of the first i characters of text1 and the first j characters of text2. When text1[i-1] == text2[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either string.
Each row only depends on the previous row, so two rows of length len(text2)+1 suffice.
signature: def longestCommonSubsequence(self, text1: str, text2: str) -> int:
approach:
**Key insight: compare the strings one prefix at a time. If the last characters of two prefixes match, they belong to a common subsequence; otherwise at least one of them can be discarded.**

Let `dp[i][j]` be the LCS length of `text1[:i]` and `text2[:j]`. Then

- `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1` if `text1[i-1] == text2[j-1]`
- `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])` otherwise

with `dp[0][*] = dp[*][0] = 0`. The answer is `dp[len1][len2]`.

**Why it is correct:** when the last characters match, some optimal common subsequence can be made to end with that pair (exchange argument), so extending the LCS of the two shorter prefixes by one is optimal. When they differ, the two last characters cannot both be the final matched pair, so dropping one of them loses nothing.

**Space optimisation:** row `i` depends only on row `i-1`, so keep two rows. With the shorter string on the inner dimension memory is `O(min(m, n))`. Recovering the subsequence itself requires the full table (walk back from the corner).

**Common mistakes:** confusing subsequence with substring (substring requires contiguity and resets to 0 on mismatch); off-by-one errors between 0-indexed characters and 1-indexed table entries; taking `dp[i-1][j-1] + 1` even when the characters differ.

**Interview follow-ups:** (1) Print one actual LCS, not just its length. (2) Edit Distance and Shortest Common Supersequence are the same table with different transitions. (3) Longest Palindromic Subsequence is LCS of a string with its reverse.
